newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - JULY 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS - JULY 24.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The 14 Greek names listed by Swiss banks in their search for heirs to accounts opened before 1945 are unlikely to be found after such a long time, the Central Council of Greek Jews reports. However, the Council said it was determined to fight for its share of the money stolen by Nazi occupation forces or extorted as ransom to save Jews from concentration camps.

--Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash is reported to be seeking a postponement of the second round of talks with Cypriot president Glafcos Clerides scheduled for August. Denktash will meet Clerides on Monday in Nicosia.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis and Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos reportedly discussed planned changes to the structure of the Greek armed forces at their meeting on Wednesday. The changes aim at transforming a top-heavy centralised mechanism into smaller rapid reaction forces.
--A legendary production of Aristophanes' "Birds" staged 38 years ago will be revived at the ancient Epidavros theatre this weekend.

--The finance ministry's planning reportedly foresees an increased tax burden on middle and high income earners to cover losses from a planned indexation of the tax scale and increase in the tax-free threshold and make up the 800 billion drachmas needed to be raised next year.

--The plot thickens in the murder Tuesday of a London-based Greek priest shot dead in a suburban Athens street. Police said Archimandrite Anthimos Eleftheriadis had willed his apartment to 42-year-old Katerina Yiannakopoulou, whom police are seeking and consider the leading suspect in the case.
--A new European Commission expected to be published soon will mean traditional Greek sweetmeats will be banned under new guidelines to protect consumers from the risk of mad cows disease.
--Development Minister Vasso Papandreou's suit against Eleftheros Typos for defamation has prompted objections from leading figures from the conservation opposition.
--Albanian bandits operating on the Greek border are thought to have begun fires in the region as a reaction to stepped up security measures. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
